name: Atacama Desert
summary: One of the driest places on Earth, with very little life in the soil and wide rocky plains. Often compared to Martian surface conditions.

landing.why: Wide flat plains, firm ground and very clear skies suit landing and optical navigation tests.

rover.why: Rocky, dusty, almost vegetation-free terrain with slopes and obstacles.

base.why: Remote, dry and with strong day–night temperature swings; road access exists for logistics.

history.what: Rover and life-detection field tests by several research teams (to verify).

whyAnalog: Extreme dryness similar to the Martian surface
Soils with very low organic content
Rocky, dusty plains with little vegetation
whatItLacks: Occasional fog and rare rain events

name: Haughton Crater, Devon Island
mirrors: Mars – polar impact crater; Moon – crater terrain
summary: An impact crater in the Canadian High Arctic, cold, dry and unvegetated. A long-running site for Mars field research.

landing.why: Rough crater terrain and difficult, weather-dependent access make repeated landing tests impractical.

rover.why: Polar desert with impact breccias, valleys and slopes.

base.why: Remote and cold, with seasonal logistic access by air.

history.what: Rover and vehicle traverse field research (to verify).
Field station and simulated habitat operations (to verify).

whyAnalog: Impact crater geology in a cold, dry setting
Isolation comparable to an early outpost
whatItLacks: Summer temperatures much warmer than Mars

name: Mars Desert Research Station, Utah
summary: A habitat in the Utah desert where crews run simulated Mars missions, surrounded by red, layered sedimentary rock.

landing.why: Badland terrain with gullies and soft clays; few large flat, firm areas.

rover.why: Varied sedimentary terrain, slopes and almost no vegetation.

base.why: Isolated desert setting with road access and an existing habitat.

history.what: Student rover competitions held near the station (to verify).

whyAnalog: Red layered sediments that look like Martian outcrops
whatItLacks: Close to towns, so isolation is partly simulated

name: HI-SEAS, Mauna Loa, Hawaii
summary: A habitat on the slopes of a large volcano, surrounded by bare basaltic lava flows. Used for long-duration isolation studies.

landing.why: Steep volcanic slopes and sharp lava; no safe flat landing zone.

rover.why: The site is set up for habitat studies; access and permits for vehicle traverses are not assumed here.

base.why: Isolated, high altitude, bare basalt and an existing dome habitat.

whyAnalog: Basaltic lava similar to lunar maria and Martian plains
High altitude and almost no vegetation
whatItLacks: Mild temperatures compared with Moon or Mars

name: Black Point Lava Flow, Arizona
summary: A basaltic lava flow in the Arizona desert used for testing exploration vehicles and procedures (Desert RATS).

landing.why: Firm basalt surfaces next to cinder fields give natural hazards for hazard-detection tests.

rover.why: Lava, cinders and slopes in a dry, accessible area.

base.why: Short-duration field site; not isolated enough for long habitat stays.

history.what: Desert RATS field tests of rovers and exploration procedures.

whyAnalog: Basaltic surface similar to lunar mare

name: Lanzarote
mirrors: Mars / Moon – volcanic plains and lava tubes
summary: A volcanic island with young lava fields, cinder cones and lava tubes, used for astronaut geology training and rover tests.

landing.why: Protected park areas and rough lava limit landing test zones.

rover.why: Varied volcanic terrain and lava tubes for mobility and cave tests.

base.why: Touristic island, not isolated enough for habitat simulation.

history.what: Rover tests and astronaut geology training (to verify).

whyAnalog: Lava tubes similar to those seen on the Moon and Mars
Little vegetation in the lava fields

name: Río Tinto
summary: A red, highly acidic, iron-rich river system. Studied as an analog for ancient Martian water chemistry and tested for drilling.

landing.why: Mining area with valleys and infrastructure; not a landing zone.

rover.why: Mineralogy and subsurface relevant for drilling and sampling rovers.

base.why: Close to towns and mines; not isolated.

history.what: Drilling and sampling technology tests (to verify).

whyAnalog: Minerals that may relate to Martian deposits
whatItLacks: Liquid water at the surface (unlike present Mars)

name: Habitat Marte, Rio Grande do Norte
summary: An analog habitat run by a Brazilian university in the semi-arid northeast (Caiçara do Rio do Vento, RN), used for simulated Mars missions and education.

landing.why: Shrubby caatinga vegetation and small terrain; no landing zone.

rover.why: Vegetation and soils limit rover analog value.

base.why: Existing habitat with simulation programme.

sources.label: Olhar Digital (2021) — news article on Habitat Marte (team-provided, secondary source)

name: Iceland lava fields
summary: Young basaltic lava fields and black sand plains, used for rover tests and astronaut geology training.

landing.why: Frequent cloud and rain limit optical navigation; lava is very rough.

rover.why: Fresh basalt, black sand plains and lava tubes.

base.why: Not isolated enough; visitors and roads nearby.

history.what: Rover field tests and astronaut geology training (to verify).

whatItLacks: Glacial processes that differ from Mars today

name: Concordia Station
mirrors: Moon / Mars – isolation and extreme cold
summary: A research station on the Antarctic plateau, isolated for months during winter. Used to study crews in extreme isolation.

landing.why: Snow and ice surface is not representative of regolith.

rover.why: Ice plateau without rocks or regolith.

base.why: Extreme cold, darkness and months of total isolation.

history.what: Winter-over isolation and crew health studies.

name: Cinder Lake Crater Field, Arizona
summary: A field of artificial craters blasted into volcanic cinders to rehearse lunar landing-site work and test rovers.

landing.why: Craters were built to mimic a lunar landing site.

rover.why: Cinders and craters for rover driving tests.

base.why: Small field near a city; no isolation.

whyAnalog: Crater pattern copied from a lunar site

name: Florida lander hazard field
mirrors: Moon – rocks and craters in a landing zone
summary: An engineered hazard field with built rocks and craters used to test autonomous lander hazard detection.

landing.why: Purpose-built field to test hazard detection during landing.

rover.why: Small engineered field inside a launch site; not natural terrain.

base.why: Inside an active launch site; no isolation.

history.what: Autonomous landing and hazard-avoidance flight tests (to verify).

whyAnalog: Rocks and craters sized for lunar landing tests

name: Vargeão crater
summary: An impact structure about 12 km wide formed in basaltic lava flows, in Santa Catarina. Rare example of an impact into basalt, as on many Martian plains. Literature cited by the team points to it as an analog for impact-driven hydrothermal activity on Mars.

landing.why: Crater rim and valleys, farms and a town inside the structure.

rover.why: Impact breccias in basalt, slopes and rim terrain for geology traverses.

base.why: A town sits inside the crater; no isolation.

whyAnalog: Impact into basalt, like many Martian craters
Shocked rocks and breccias for sampling practice

sources.label: Icarus 252 (2015) 347–365 — Vargeão as Mars impact-hydrothermal analog (team-provided, verify)

name: Vista Alegre crater
summary: An impact structure about 9.5 km wide in basalt, in Paraná, similar in setting to Vargeão.

landing.why: Farmland and rolling terrain; no open landing zone.

rover.why: Impact rocks in basalt for sampling and navigation exercises.

base.why: Agricultural area, not isolated.

name: Cerro do Jarau
mirrors: Mars – crater with sedimentary and volcanic layers
summary: A circular structure in Rio Grande do Sul, in basalt and sandstone, studied as an impact crater in the Pampa.

landing.why: Grassland is fine for vehicles but the crater hills make the zone uneven.

rover.why: Mixed sandstone and basalt with hills for geology traverses.

base.why: Ranch land with roads; low isolation and mild climate.

whyAnalog: Impact into layered sandstone and basalt
Ring-shaped hills useful for navigation tests

name: Araguainha crater
mirrors: Moon / Mars – complex crater with central uplift
summary: The largest known impact structure in South America (about 40 km), on the Goiás–Mato Grosso border, with a central uplift.

landing.why: Cerrado vegetation and complex relief.

rover.why: Central uplift, rings and varied rocks for long geology traverses.

base.why: Not extreme enough: mild temperatures and nearby towns.

whyAnalog: Complex crater with central uplift, like many lunar and Martian craters

name: Serra da Cangalha
summary: A well-defined impact crater about 13 km wide in Tocantins, with a clear ring of hills.

landing.why: Ring hills and vegetation; landing zone not flat.

rover.why: Clear crater rim and central area for traverses.

base.why: Remote area with hot dry season and limited access.

name: Lençóis Maranhenses
summary: A large field of white sand dunes with seasonal freshwater lagoons between them, in Maranhão.

landing.why: Moving dunes and lagoons; soft surface.

rover.why: Large dune field for testing mobility in loose sand (dry season).

base.why: National park with protected status and tourism.

whyAnalog: Wind-shaped forms similar to Martian dunes

name: Raso da Catarina
summary: A dry sandstone plateau in Bahia with sandy soils and canyons, one of the driest parts of the Brazilian caatinga.

landing.why: Flat sandy plateau with low slopes.

rover.why: Sand, canyons and slopes for mobility tests.

base.why: Protected ecological area; habitat permits uncertain.

name: Salar de Uyuni
mirrors: Mars – evaporite basins; Moon – flat landing plains
summary: The largest salt flat on Earth, extremely flat and high (about 3,600 m), with cold nights and strong sunlight.

landing.why: Extremely flat and firm surface for landing and navigation tests.

rover.why: Too flat and uniform: few rocks or slopes to challenge a rover.

base.why: High altitude, cold nights, isolation and salts for ISRU experiments.

whyAnalog: Evaporite salts like some Martian basins
High altitude, strong UV and cold nights

name: Puna de Atacama
summary: A very high, dry volcanic plateau with salt flats, lava and strong winds. Thin air and big temperature swings.

landing.why: Wide flat areas, clear skies and thin air.

rover.why: Volcanic rocks, sand and slopes with almost no vegetation.

base.why: Isolation, cold, thin air and local resources for ISRU tests.

whyAnalog: Very high altitude and thin air
whatItLacks: Atmosphere still much thicker than Mars

name: Jalapão
summary: A remote region in Tocantins with orange dunes, sandstone mesas and sparse vegetation.

landing.why: Soft sand and mesas; no firm landing zone.

rover.why: Dunes and sandstone slopes for mobility tests.

base.why: Remote, with limited access and a long dry season.
